parameters.label: Seconds staring at the red
parameters.explain: The longer the cone cells see one colour, the more they adapt — and the stronger the afterimage.

parameters.label: Seconds since she looked at the wall
parameters.explain: Away from the red, the tired cones slowly return to normal and the ghost fades.

parameters.label: Colour she stares at
parameters.explain: The twist: the ghost is always the opposite colour of what she stared at. It's made by her eyes and brain, not by anything on the wall.

parameters.label: Her eyes while staring
parameters.explain: Wandering eyes spread the red over different cells, so no cells get as tired and the ghost is weak and blurry.

parameters.label: How vivid the red is
parameters.explain: Stronger, higher-contrast colours tire the cones more.

parameters.label: What she looks at afterwards
parameters.explain: On a white surface the fresh cones respond strongly, so the opposite colour stands out most.

overlay.caption: staring at red → red-sensing cones tire → on white, the fresh cones win → a green ghost that follows her eyes

explain.summary: Hana's eyes have cone cells that sense red, green and blue light, and her brain turns their signals into colour. Two minutes of bright red tired her red-sensing cones. On the white wall, the fresh green-sensing cones answer more strongly than the tired red ones, so her brain sees green — a colour that isn't there. As the tired cones recover, the ghost fades in about twenty seconds.
rules: Tiredness builds up the longer she stares, halving the gap to fully tired every 15 seconds.
Vivid colour and eyes held still make the cones more tired.
The ghost is the opposite colour: red → green, green → reddish-pink, blue → yellow, yellow → blue.
After she looks away the ghost halves every 2–6 seconds (slower after a long stare) and is brightest on white.

source.fact: Light bleaches cone cells; staring at red tires the red cones while the green cones stay fresh, so on a white background the green cones respond more and the afterimage is the complementary colour. After long exposure it takes a little while for the cones to return to normal.
Cones exposed to the same colour for too long get fatigued and other cones take over; the colour of a negative afterimage is the complementary colour, and it can be seen for several seconds.
The longer and stronger the adapting image, the larger the effect on the after-image; the chance of an after-image increases with adaptation time, and higher-contrast colours make adaptation easier.
Photoreceptors in the retina turn light into electrical signals that travel through the optic nerve to the brain, which turns them into the images we see.

choice.what: Cone tiredness builds with a 15-second half-time
choice.why: Chosen so a 20–30 second stare (as in common demos) gives a clear ghost and two minutes gives nearly the maximum.

choice.what: The ghost fades with a half-time of 2–6 seconds, longer after a longer stare
choice.why: Matches Hana's clue (about 20 seconds after two minutes) and the sources' 'several seconds'.

choice.what: 'Lasts' means until the ghost drops below strength 1, worked out with a close approximation of a logarithm
choice.why: The model tool has no log function, so we use the standard power approximation.

choice.what: Wandering eyes cut tiredness to about 15%
choice.why: Moving the image around spreads the load over many cells; the exact amount varies.

illustrative: Hana is fictional; the 0–10 ghost strength scale is made up.
Real afterimage colours are close to, but not exactly, the opposite colour, and differ a little between people.
provenance.studying: Scientists still debate how much of an afterimage comes from tired cones in the eye and how much from adaptation further along in the brain.

citations.title: Aftereffects
citations.supports: Light bleaches cones; the red cones get tired while the green cones are still fresh; negative afterimages show the complementary colour; on a white background the green cones respond more; after long exposure cones take a while to return to normal.

citations.title: How afterimages play tricks on your eyes
citations.supports: Cones exposed to the same colour for too long get tired (fatigued) and other cones take over; a negative afterimage is the complementary colour, e.g. a red apple leaves a green afterimage; it may be seen for several seconds.

citations.title: Research article on after-image formation, DOI 10.3758/s13414-022-02570-8
citations.supports: The probability of after-image formation increases with adaptation duration; the longer and the stronger the adapter, the larger the effect on the after-image; higher-contrast colours facilitate adaptation.

citations.title: How the Eyes Work
citations.supports: Photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals, which travel from the retina through the optic nerve to the brain; the brain turns the signals into the images you see.

does: Shows colour-sensing cells tiring the longer and harder they work
Shows the ghost is always the opposite colour, made inside the eye and brain
Shows the ghost fading as the cells recover
doesnt: Measure any real person — Hana is fictional and the numbers are illustrative
Cover colour blindness or the brain's colour processing in detail
Suggest staring at bright lights or the sun — never do that
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Afterimages from paint or paper fade in seconds. If spots in your vision don't fade, tell an adult.
